text.p: BRUSSELS, April 23 (Reuter) The European Commission said on Wednesday it was investigating a 1993 deal under which Philips Electronics sold technical know-how to Rabobank and then leased it back again.
It said the probe would look at whether the operation, which resulted in a much-needed cash injection for Philips and tax benefits for Rabobank, involved an element of illegal state aid.

"Additional information is indispensable and the Commission will therefore address a letter to the Dutch authorities requesting full disclosure of the fiscal treatment of the technolease transaction of Philips and Rabobank," it said.
At the end of 1993, Philips sold know-how to Rabobank for 2.78 billion guilders, of which 600 million guilders was paid immediately by the bank, the Commission said in a statement.
Rabobank leased the know-how back to Philips for a period of 10 years, agreeing to pay the bank an annual royalty of 140 million guilders.
Rabobank is also entitled to half of the proceeds resulting from licences granted to other companies on the basis of the know-how, the statement added.
Sale and lease back transactions, which are common for tangible assets in the aerospace and real estate sectors, are usually subject to special tax treatment.
But the transaction between Philips and Rabobank was unusual because it involved intangible assets.
The Commission said it needed to investigate whether tax regulations had been correctly applied in this case.
Commission investigations into possible cases of illegal state aid are not subject to a formal deadline.
